0.title: The Household of God
0.essay:
Many Christians today think of church as optional: a helpful resource for their personal faith, to be used when convenient. Some have been hurt by churches and keep their distance. Others move from church to church looking for the right music or programmes. Yet the New Testament speaks of the church in the highest terms.

Bought with blood

It is “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). To love Christ is to love what he loves.

The church is not a building, a denomination or a weekly event. It is a people: those whom God has called out of the world to belong to Christ and to each other. And it is not an invention of Christians. Jesus said, “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). It is his project, and it cannot fail.

What this study covers

This study asks what the church is, why belonging matters, how it is led, what baptism and the Lord’s Supper mean, and how a church keeps its purity, unity and mission. Where Christians disagree — on church government, baptism and the Lord’s Supper — the main views are set out before a verdict is given.

The chapters

What Is the Church?; Belonging — why every Christian needs a church; Shepherds and Servants — elders and deacons; Baptism; The Lord’s Supper; and Purity, Unity and Mission. The Worship and the Lord’s Day study covers what happens when the church gathers on Sunday.

1.title: What Is the Church?
1.essay:
Peter had just confessed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus answered with a promise: “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). He calls it “my church”. It belongs to him, he builds it, and he guarantees it.

A people

The New Testament uses many pictures for the church, and each shows something different. It is a people: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). Peter takes the titles given to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6) and applies them to the church of Jews and Gentiles together. Those who were once not a people are now God’s people, and their purpose is mission.

The church does not replace Israel as if God had changed his plans. Believing Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree of God’s people (Romans 11:17–24). The church is the one people of God, now made up of Jew and Gentile together in Christ.

A family and a temple

Paul uses three pictures in quick succession: “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). A nation, a family, and then a building: the church “grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:21–22). God is our Father, Christ our elder brother, and other believers our brothers and sisters. That is not sentimental language; it means real obligations of love, care, honesty and loyalty.

And God’s presence, once found in the temple in Jerusalem, now lives in his gathered people. The temple is still growing. Every believer is a stone being fitted into place — “like living stones … being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5) — and Christ is the cornerstone that holds it together.

A body and a bride

“Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Christ is the head; believers are the members, each with a different function, all needing each other. The church at Corinth was divided by rivalry and spiritual pride, and Paul reminded them that they had all been baptised into one body by one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). Unity in the church is not something we create. The Spirit has created it, and we must keep it.

And the church is a bride. Christ loves her as a husband loves his wife, and is preparing her for the wedding day, “so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27).

Christ and his church

Saul of Tarsus was persecuting Christians when the risen Jesus stopped him on the road and asked, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Not “my people”, but “me”. Christ so identifies with his church that to harm it is to harm him.

Universal and local

The universal church is all true believers of every time and place, known fully only to God. The local church is a particular gathering of believers in one place, committed to one another under Christ. Most New Testament uses of “church” mean local congregations: the church in Corinth, the church that meets in someone’s house. In practice you cannot belong to the universal church except by belonging to a local one.

The church as God sees it is all the elect, everyone who truly belongs to Christ. The church as we see it is those who profess faith. They overlap but are not identical; some who profess are not genuine (1 John 2:19), and the church on earth is always mixed. That is why the church must exercise care, though it cannot read hearts.

The marks of a true church

The Reformers asked how to recognise a true church amid corruption. They answered with three marks: the faithful preaching of the word of God, the right administration of baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and the exercise of church discipline. A gathering without these may have a building and a crowd, but it lacks what makes a church a church.

A hand cut off

A young professional has watched online sermons for two years without going to a church. She thinks of herself as a committed Christian. Reading Ephesians, she realises that its pictures are all corporate: a body, a household, a temple. She cannot be a hand cut off from the body. She starts attending a local church, and within months finds friendship and accountability she did not know she was missing.

If your church disappeared tomorrow, would anyone notice you were missing? Would you miss them?

For reflection

Which picture of the church — people, family, temple, body or bride — speaks most to you, and why? Why do both the universal and the local church matter? Read Acts 9:1–5: what does it tell you about how Christ sees his church? How would you explain to a friend why church is not optional for a Christian?

2.title: Belonging: Why Every Christian Needs a Church
2.essay:
The first Christians did not attend church; they belonged to it. After Pentecost, those who believed were baptised and added to the church, “And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). Their faith was corporate from the start.

The first church

This is the earliest snapshot of a local church. Believers gave themselves to four things: teaching, fellowship, the Lord’s Supper and prayer. They shared generously, met daily and praised God. “And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:47). Growth was the Lord’s work, through a devoted and loving community. Their belonging was not just a name on a list. It showed in their wallets, homes and time: “There was not a needy person among them” (Acts 4:34).

Why membership?

The phrase “church membership” is not in the Bible, but the reality is everywhere. The New Testament assumes that believers are known and counted in local churches. Paul writes to particular churches. Elders are told to “shepherd the flock of God that is among you” (1 Peter 5:2), so they must know who is in it. Church discipline requires knowing who is inside and who is outside (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). And the “one another” commands — love, bear with, encourage, admonish, serve — need specific people to be obeyed with. Membership simply makes visible a commitment the New Testament assumes.

What belonging gives

A church gives us teaching we would not choose for ourselves, so that we hear the whole counsel of God. It gives us people who know us well enough to encourage and warn us. It gives us a place to use our gifts. It gives us the sacraments, which belong to the gathered church. And it gives us shepherds, who “are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account” (Hebrews 13:17). That is a sobering responsibility, and members are called to follow their leaders so that the work is a joy and not a burden.

Paul uses the body picture again in Romans 12: many members, different functions, one body. Each believer has gifts — prophesying, serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy — and each is to use them (Romans 12:4–8). A church works best when every member serves, not when a few professionals do everything.

What belonging asks

It asks faithfulness: “not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another” (Hebrews 10:25). The writer joins three things: hold fast to hope, stir one another up to love and good works, and keep meeting. They belong together. Christians who drift from the gathered church usually drift from hope and good works as well.

Belonging also asks service, giving, prayer and patience with imperfect people. It asks the humility to receive correction and to follow godly leaders. And it asks us to stay through difficult seasons rather than moving on at the first disappointment.

A couple have moved churches four times in eight years, each time because something disappointed them. Reading Hebrews 10:24–25, they realise they have treated church as a consumer product. They commit to their current church, join a small group, start serving with the children, and resolve to take concerns to the elders directly instead of leaving. Five years later they are among its most valued members.

Choosing a church

Look first for the marks of a true church. Is the Bible faithfully taught? Is the gospel clear? Are baptism and the Lord’s Supper rightly practised? Are the leaders qualified and accountable? Is there real care for members? Music style, programmes and convenience matter far less. No church is perfect — and if you find one, joining it will spoil it.

Hard questions

The old saying “outside the church there is no salvation” has been misused to mean that a particular institution controls salvation. That is false; salvation is through faith in Christ alone. But it expresses a truth: God saves people into a people. A believer who deliberately refuses fellowship with other believers is acting against the nature of the new life he has received (1 John 4:20).

When should you leave a church? Serious reasons include the abandonment of the gospel, persistent false teaching, abuse by leaders that the church will not address, or a move to another place. Preferences about style are not good reasons. When you do leave, do it honestly and peaceably, speaking to the leaders rather than slipping away.

Recorded sermons can be a blessing to the housebound and to those far from a faithful church. But they cannot replace the gathered body, where believers see, serve, encourage and are known by one another.

Who in your church knows you well enough to warn you if you were drifting from Christ?

For reflection

Are you a member of a local church? If not, what is holding you back? Read Acts 2:42–47: which of these marks is strongest in your church, and which is weakest? What do you give to your church, and what do you receive? What would it mean for you to be more committed to it this year?

3.title: Shepherds and Servants: Elders and Deacons
3.essay:
Christ, the head of the church, gives it leaders to care for it. The New Testament names two ongoing offices: elders, also called overseers or pastors, and deacons.

Elders are shepherds

Paul told the elders of Ephesus, “Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). Watch yourselves first, then the flock. Remember that the Spirit appointed you and that the church was bought with God’s own blood. Then he warned them that wolves would come, from outside and from within. Guarding the flock against false teaching is one of an elder’s most important tasks.

Their work is to teach the word, to pray, to guard the church and to watch over its members. Peter, an apostle, calls himself “a fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1). He tells elders to shepherd willingly, not for money, “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). They answer to the Chief Shepherd, who will reward faithful service. Then Peter tells younger members to be subject to the elders, and everyone to clothe themselves with humility. Healthy churches need humble leaders and humble members.

When Paul said farewell to the Ephesian elders, he reminded them that he had served with tears, taught publicly and from house to house, and coveted no one’s silver or gold. Then he knelt and prayed with them, “And there was much weeping on the part of all” (Acts 20:37). That is what shepherding looks like.

Character first

“If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task” (1 Timothy 3:1). But Paul’s lists in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are striking. Almost every qualification is about character: above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his household well, well thought of by outsiders. Only one is about skill: “able to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2). The list is not a demand for perfection, but for maturity and a good reputation. A man who cannot care for his own household cannot care for God’s church, and a recent convert should not be appointed, lest he become proud.

Churches often choose leaders for success or charisma. God chooses them for godliness. A church is choosing new elders. One candidate is a successful businessman and confident speaker, but harsh with his family and known for a quick temper. Another is a quiet schoolteacher whose home is peaceful and who has faithfully led a Bible study for years. Reading 1 Timothy 3 together, the church sees which one Scripture points to.

A plurality

In the New Testament, churches were led by a group of elders, not a single pastor (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5; James 5:14). Some elders labour especially in preaching and teaching (1 Timothy 5:17), but all share in the oversight. A plurality guards against one man’s blind spots and pride.

Deacons

The first serious problem in the church was a complaint that some widows were being neglected. The apostles did not ignore it, but neither did they abandon prayer and preaching to fix it themselves: “we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4). They asked the church to choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to take on the work. Practical care mattered so much that it needed spiritual men. And the result was that “the word of God continued to increase” (Acts 6:7). Deacons are servants who lead in practical care, freeing elders to shepherd, and their qualifications too are mainly about character (1 Timothy 3:8–13).

Male elders

Scripture restricts the office of elder to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:2). That is not because women are less gifted or less valuable, but because of God’s design for the church family, grounded in creation (1 Timothy 2:13). The studies on Biblical Manhood and Biblical Womanhood explore this further.

How should a church be governed?

Episcopal churches are governed by bishops over many congregations. Presbyterian churches are governed by elders, with local elders accountable to regional and national assemblies. Congregational churches govern themselves, with the members holding final authority under Christ, often led by elders.

The New Testament pattern is a plurality of qualified elders leading each local church, with the congregation involved in key decisions. The church chose the seven in Acts 6:3, and it is the church that acts in discipline (Matthew 18:17; 1 Corinthians 5:4). Churches also rightly cooperate for counsel and mission, as at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15). The fixed points are that Christ is the head, Scripture is the rule, and leaders must be qualified and accountable.

Pray for them

Elders are sinners like everyone else, and they carry a heavy burden. Paul repeatedly asked churches to pray for him (Ephesians 6:19; Colossians 4:3). Encourage your leaders, pray for them, and bring your concerns to them directly. When did you last pray by name for the elders of your church?

For reflection

Why do you think almost all the qualifications for elders are about character? What are the benefits of several elders over a single pastor? Read 1 Peter 5:1–5: what does it ask of leaders, and what of members? How can you encourage the leaders of your church this week?

4.title: Baptism
4.essay:
Jesus’ last command to his disciples included baptism: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20). Baptism is not optional for Christians. It is the Lord’s command and the sign of entry into his church.

The start of discipleship

Jesus’ authority is the ground of the command. Making disciples includes baptising them and teaching them, so baptism marks the beginning of discipleship, not its end. It is done in the one name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, bringing the believer into relationship with the whole Trinity. And the promise follows: Jesus will be with his people to the end.

What it means

Baptism pictures union with Christ in his death and resurrection: “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). Paul uses it to answer the question whether Christians should keep sinning so that grace may abound. No, because in baptism we were united to Christ’s death and resurrection. It marks the end of the old life and the start of the new. To return to sin is to deny what our baptism signifies.

Baptism also pictures cleansing from sin: “Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name” (Acts 22:16). It marks entry into the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13). And because it is done in God’s name, it places the baptised person under his ownership and claim.

More than a testimony

Baptism is sometimes described as simply a public statement of someone’s decision. It is a public confession, but it is more. It is God’s covenant sign, administered by the church in his name, declaring his promise to all who believe and claiming them as his. It is about what God has done before it is about what we have done.

What it does not do

Baptism does not cause the new birth. The thief on the cross was saved without it (Luke 23:43). Simon the magician was baptised without being saved (Acts 8:13, 20–23). Paul connects baptism with “a circumcision made without hands” — Christ cutting away the old nature — and says we were “buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith” (Colossians 2:11–12). The spiritual reality comes through faith, and baptism signifies it. Yet that does not make baptism unimportant. A believer who refuses baptism is disobeying Christ.

Mode

Christians have baptised by immersion, pouring and sprinkling. Immersion best pictures burial and resurrection with Christ, and fits the New Testament descriptions of going down into the water and coming up out of it (Acts 8:38–39). But the meaning of baptism does not depend on the amount of water.

Who should be baptised?

Most of the historic Reformed tradition, along with Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches, baptises the infants of believers. Reformed paedobaptists argue from the unity of the covenant of grace: the children of believers received the covenant sign of circumcision in the Old Testament, and baptism has replaced circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12). Whole households were baptised in Acts (Acts 16:15, 33). And Peter said, “the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39).

Reformed credobaptists hold that baptism is for those who profess faith, because the new covenant is made with those who know the Lord.

Believer’s baptism is the more faithful position. The new covenant promises that “they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11). Peter’s promise was for “everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (Acts 2:39), and it was “those who received his word” who were baptised (Acts 2:41). Every baptism the New Testament describes follows repentance and faith. The household baptisms do not mention infants; in Philippi the word was first spoken “to all who were in his house”, and the whole household rejoiced “that he had believed in God” (Acts 16:32–34). Baptism signifies union with Christ by faith, which belongs to those who believe. Paedobaptists are dear brothers and sisters, and the Covenant Theology study sets out both cases more fully.

Children of Christian parents are greatly privileged. They hear the gospel, are prayed for and are raised in the church. They should be taught to trust Christ from their earliest days, and baptised when they credibly profess faith.

What prevents me?

An Ethiopian official was reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot when Philip explained it to him. As they came to some water, he asked, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36). They went down into the water, Philip baptised him, and he “went on his way rejoicing” (Acts 8:39). Faith, then baptism, then joy.

A woman became a Christian in her forties but has put off baptism because she is shy and dreads standing in front of the church. Reading Matthew 28, she sees it as obedience to Christ rather than a performance. On the day her voice shakes as she confesses her faith. Afterwards, many in the church embrace her. She belongs.

If you are a believer who has not been baptised, what is holding you back from obeying Christ in this?

For reflection

What does baptism mean according to Romans 6:3–5? Why is it more than a personal testimony? How would you explain your view of infant baptism, graciously, to a Christian who disagrees? If you have been baptised, how does remembering it encourage you to live for Christ?

5.title: The Lord’s Supper
5.essay:
On the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread and wine and gave them a new meaning. “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” And the cup: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:19–20). He gave his church a meal to keep until he returns.

A greater exodus

Jesus was eating the Passover with his disciples, the meal that remembered Israel’s rescue from Egypt by the blood of a lamb. Now he gave it a new focus: his own body given and his blood poured out. The new covenant promised through Jeremiah is established by his death. Every Lord’s Supper remembers a greater exodus. And the Supper faces in four directions.

Looking back: remembrance

The Supper calls us to remember Christ’s death, not as a distant event but as the sacrifice by which we are saved. Paul hands on what he “received from the Lord” — among the oldest written words about the Supper — and adds, “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). Every time the church eats and drinks, it preaches the gospel.

Looking up: communion

“The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). Paul was warning against idolatry: those who share the Lord’s table cannot also share in idol feasts. His argument assumes that the Supper is a real participation in Christ, not a mere symbol. In it believers truly feed on Christ by faith. It is a means of grace, through which the Spirit strengthens our faith and deepens our union with him.

Looking around: fellowship

“Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). It is a family meal. Divisions and contempt for other believers contradict what it declares, which is why Paul rebuked the Corinthians so severely for humiliating poorer members at the table (1 Corinthians 11:20–22).

Looking forward: hope

Jesus said he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until the kingdom of God comes (Luke 22:18). Every Lord’s Supper is a foretaste of the wedding feast: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). The Supper carries a horizon: “until he comes”.

Coming worthily

Paul warns against eating “in an unworthy manner” (1 Corinthians 11:27). That does not mean only those who feel worthy may come; no one is worthy. It means coming without discerning the body — with careless contempt for Christ and his people, or with unrepented sin. The Corinthians had been doing exactly that, and God had disciplined some with sickness and even death. The remedy is self-examination: “Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28). And even God’s discipline has a loving purpose, “so that we may not be condemned along with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:32). The Supper is for repentant sinners, not for the perfect.

A believer has always found communion awkward. She is not sure what to think about, and often wonders whether she is worthy enough. Her pastor explains that the Supper is not a test of worthiness but a gift for the weak. Next time she confesses her sins, looks to Christ crucified and risen, and receives the bread and cup as his gift to her. For the first time, it feels like a meal.

How is Christ present?

Roman Catholic teaching holds that the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), and that the Mass is a sacrifice. Lutherans hold that Christ’s body and blood are present “in, with and under” the bread and wine. Many evangelicals hold that the Supper is a memorial only, a reminder of Christ’s death. The Reformed view holds that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and that believers truly feed on him by faith, while the bread and wine remain bread and wine.

The Reformed view fits the whole of Scripture best. “This is my body” is like “I am the door”: a sign that represents a reality. Christ’s body is now in heaven, “whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things” (Acts 3:21), and his sacrifice was “once for all” (Hebrews 10:10), so it cannot be repeated in a Mass. Yet Paul calls the Supper a real participation in Christ, more than a memory. Christ meets his people at his table by his Spirit, and faith receives him.

On the evening of the resurrection, two disciples walked to Emmaus with a stranger. At supper “he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him” (Luke 24:30–31). Christ makes himself known in the breaking of bread.

Who may come?

The Supper is for baptised believers who are walking in repentance. Children who have not yet professed faith, and unbelievers, should not take it, though they may be present and should be lovingly taught what it means.

When you take the Lord’s Supper, do you come as someone performing a ritual, or as someone being fed by Christ?

For reflection

What do the four directions of the Supper — back, up, around and forward — teach you? What does it mean to eat “in an unworthy manner”? How would you explain the Reformed view of Christ’s presence? How can you prepare your heart before the next Lord’s Supper?

6.title: Purity, Unity and Mission
6.essay:
Every healthy church holds three things together: purity, unity and mission. Without purity, unity becomes compromise. Without unity, purity becomes harshness. And without mission, both turn inward.

Purity: discipline that restores

Church discipline is the loving correction of members who persist in serious sin. It begins privately and gently: “Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1). Those who restore must watch themselves, lest they too are tempted, and bearing one another’s burdens fulfils the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2). Discipline begins not with a church meeting but with one believer gently helping another.

If a member refuses to repent of serious, public sin, Jesus and Paul teach that the church must finally remove him from membership (Matthew 18:17; 1 Corinthians 5:13). That sounds harsh, but its aims are loving. It seeks to bring the sinner to repentance, “so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5:5). It protects the church: “Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?” (1 Corinthians 5:6). Tolerated sin spreads. And it guards Christ’s honour before the world: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and his church must live as his holy people.

Discipline is not punishment. The church does not punish sin; Christ has borne the punishment for his people. Discipline is a warning and a call to come back. It treats sin as seriously as God does, and the sinner as lovingly as God does. The door is always open.

In Corinth a man was living with his father’s wife, and the church was proud of its tolerance. Paul commanded discipline. In his next letter he speaks of a disciplined man, perhaps the same one, who had repented, and he urges the church to forgive and comfort him: “So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him” (2 Corinthians 2:8). Discipline had worked as it was meant to.

Unity: keeping the peace

Paul begs believers to walk worthy of their calling “with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2–3). Unity is already given by the Spirit; our task is to keep it. It is not uniformity, and it is not achieved by ignoring truth. It rests on the great “ones”: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Ephesians 4:4–6). Within that faith, Christians must bear with one another’s differences, weaknesses and preferences.

That requires telling different kinds of truth apart. First-order truths — the gospel, the Trinity, the person of Christ — define the faith. Second-order matters, such as baptism and church government, may require separate churches. Third-order matters, such as music style or details of the end times, should never divide a church.

A church disagrees bitterly over a change in worship style, and some threaten to leave. The elders call the church to read Ephesians 4:1–16 together, to repent of harsh words and to remember what unites them. The disagreement is not fully resolved, but people choose to bear with one another, and the church stays together.

Unity is evangelistic

On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for all who would believe through the apostles’ word — which includes us — that they would be one as the Father and the Son are one, “so that the world may believe that you have sent me” (John 17:21). Divided churches undermine their witness. United churches commend the gospel.

Mission: the church sent

The church exists not only for itself but for the world. Christ has given it the task of making disciples of all nations. That happens through faithful preaching, through members speaking of Christ in daily life, through supporting missionaries and planting churches, and through deeds of love that “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (Titus 2:10).

Growing up together

God gives the church teachers “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12), so that the whole body grows to maturity, “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). A mature church is not one with a famous pastor, but one in which every member is growing and serving.

Love her as she is

The church on earth is flawed and often disappointing. But Christ is making her holy, and one day she will be presented “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). Love the church as she is, because of what Christ will make her.

Are you more likely to break the unity of your church by insisting on your preferences, or to weaken its purity by avoiding hard conversations?

For reflection

Why is church discipline an act of love, and how can it go wrong? Read Ephesians 4:1–16: what does it say about unity and maturity? Which matters should never divide a church, and which may require separate churches? What is one way you could strengthen the unity or mission of your church this month?
